title.en: The Story of Zaragoza: The Thief the King Could Not Catch
title.zh: 薩拉戈薩傳：國王抓不到的賊

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8a 'The Story of Zaragoza', eBook #8299

summary.en: Godfather to his friend Luis's infant son, the stranger Zaragoza joins him in tunneling into the king's treasury to punish the tax-burdening monarch. Luis is killed by a hidden arrow-trap, and Zaragoza, severing the head to hide the identity, outwits every royal snare: the widow's cry explained as his own, the soldiers drugged into sleep as a priest, the decoy gold sheep rendered untraceable by marking every door with a cross. Pardoned, he tricks the richest merchant with a 'Si'-saying fool dressed as a bishop, and abducts the hermit Tubal in an iron cage disguised as a gate of heaven — winning a knighthood.
summary.zh: 陌生人薩拉戈薩為教子之父，與友人路易斯同謀掘通王庫以懲暴君。路易斯誤中箭阱身亡；薩拉戈薩割其首以免身份敗露，此後一一破解王室圈套：寡婦的哀哭被他解釋為責子、扮神父以藥酒催眠衛兵、在滿城門戶畫上同樣的十字使金羊誘餌失效。國王赦免並重用他；他以說『Si』的傻瓜假扮主教騙取富商貨物，又以鐵籠假作天門『接引』隱士入宮——終獲冊封為騎士。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Manila narrator; archival record. A Rhampsinitus + Master Thief combination; Fansler compares Groome's gypsy 'The Two Thieves' and Herodotus ii, 121.

passages.text: Poor Luis, whose three children had died unbaptized, hastened to church with his newborn son and, in haste, asked a passing stranger to stand godfather; the child was named Luis after his father, and the godfather, Zaragoza, soon won the confidence of the household as a close friend. Hearing from Luis how the king oppressed the people with heavy taxes, Zaragoza resolved to avenge the wrongs of the people by stealing the treasure hidden in a cellar of the palace. Night after night the two carried away as many bags as they could manage, Zaragoza giving his share freely to the poor while the selfish Luis admonished him not to be too liberal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'The Story of Zaragoza'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the king noticed his treasure dwindling, soldiers found the secret passage; the friends, resolved on one last trip, found it undisturbed — but as Luis lowered himself into the hole, the whiz of an arrow was heard and a faint cry: 'I am dying! Take care of my son!' Unable to pull the body free, Zaragoza shrewdly cut off the dead man's head and hurried home with it, lest Luis be recognized. When the king decreed that the headless body be carried through the streets, soldiers arresting anyone who showed sympathy for the dead man, Maria's cry of 'O my husband!' at the window betrayed her — until Zaragoza smilingly told the guard the remark was meant for himself, having unintentionally hurt their young son. The soldiers believed him and went on.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'The Story of Zaragoza'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Disguised as a priest with a bottle of wine mixed with a strong narcotic, Zaragoza that night passed himself off as a pious traveler among the soldiers, who drank freely and fell asleep; he stole the corpse and buried it with the head. The king's next stratagem — a sheep covered with precious metal let loose in the streets, a spy marking the door of anyone who caught it — failed when Zaragoza drove it into his yard and then marked every door in the street with a cross. Giving up all hope of catching the thief, the king issued a proclamation of pardon, and Zaragoza confessed and was believed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'The Story of Zaragoza'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king, promising a title of nobility if Zaragoza could trick Don Juan, the richest merchant, out of his most valuable goods, watched Zaragoza dress a fool in the guise of a bishop, asking him 'Does your grace wish to have this?' to every question, the fool's answer being always 'Si.' The carriage was loaded and Zaragoza drove off 'to fetch the money.' Next, ordered to bring an old hermit to the palace, Zaragoza placed an iron cage near the mouth of Tubal's cave and, in the guise of an angel on a high cliff, shouted that the gates of heaven were open: 'Go enter that cage, and you will see the way to heaven.' The meek hermit obeyed — and was carried before the king. Thoroughly satisfied, the king knighted Zaragoza and placed him among the chief advisers of the kingdom, where he lived with Maria and his godson under his protection as the most upright and generous man of the realm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'The Story of Zaragoza'; not verbatim.

region.en: Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province; tale set in Africa)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉；故事背景在非洲）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8b 'Juan the Peerless Robber', eBook #8299

summary.en: The famous brigand Juan flees to Africa, where he beats the Ethiopian robber Pedro at pickpocketing by unbuckling his belt. Hearing the King of Tunis reward the captor of the greatest robber alive, Juan robs the palace of one small bag, then lures his friend Pedro to jump into a tub of boiling water — collecting the reward for Pedro's own head. Disguised as an angel with two strong wings, he 'carries to heaven' a devout abbot, money-bag and all, to his cave; but the abbot's counsel reforms him, and they live together till death.
summary.zh: 大盜胡安亡命非洲，以解帶之術勝過衣索比亞同行佩德羅。突尼斯國王懸賞捉拿『國中第一大盜』；胡安先從王宮偷走一小袋財寶，再引佩德羅跳入他預置的滾水大盆——以故友的人頭領賞。之後他假扮天使、縛雙翼，從教堂穹頂將虔誠修道院長連人帶財寶『接引上天』至其洞穴；院長規勸他棄惡從善，二人同居至死。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Batangas narrator; archival record. Master-Thief cycle; Fansler compares the Persian Bahar-i-Danush. The tale's European/charlemagne framing is retained as recorded.

passages.text: Not many centuries after Charlemagne died, there lived a famous brigand named Juan, known from childhood as 'the deceitful Juan,' 'the unrivalled pilferer,' 'the treacherous Juan.' Forced at twenty to flee his native land, he visited Africa, where he met the famous Ethiopian robber Pedro; disputing which was the more skilful pickpocket, they stood face to face. 'Hey!' exclaimed Juan as Pedro began, 'don't take my handkerchief out of my pocket!' Then Juan unbuckled Pedro's belt and slipped it into his own pocket: 'Whose belt is this?' Pedro generously admitted defeat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'Juan the Peerless Robber'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Traveling in northern Africa, they heard the heralds of the King of Tunis proclaim that a big bag of money would be given to the captor of the greatest robber in the country. That night Juan climbed to the palace roof, made a hole as large as a peso, lowered himself by rope into a room filled with bags of gold and silver, pearls, carbuncles, diamonds, and other precious stones, and took the smallest bag he could find. When Pedro resolved to visit the palace the following night, Juan lowered a large tub through the same hole by day and filled it with boiling water at nightfall; the eager Pedro jumped straight into the room without the rope and perished in the fatal tub. Juan notified the king of the capture and death of the greatest of African robbers: 'Take your bag of money,' said the king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'Juan the Peerless Robber'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Juan then heard that a wealthy and devout abbot had been praying two days and nights for the angel of the Lord to come and take him to heaven. Providing himself with two strong wings, Juan made a hole through the dome of the church and called down, 'I have been sent by the Lord to take you to heaven. Come with me, and bring all your wealth.' The abbot put all his money into a bag, got into it at Juan's bidding, and after an hour's 'flight' — 'We are within one thousand miles of the abode of the blessed' — twenty minutes later they were in Juan's cave. Astounded, the abbot heard Juan's story and advised him to abandon his evil ways; Juan listened to the counsels of his new friend, became a good man, and he and the abbot lived together until their death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 8 'Juan the Peerless Robber'; not verbatim.

region.en: Mangaldan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省曼加爾丹（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pangasinan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 9 'The Seven Crazy Fellows', eBook #8299

summary.en: Seven happy fools go fishing; Juan counts six, forgetting himself, and all dive for the drowned companion until an old man counts them properly and takes them into his service. Each fails his task: Felipe hangs his hat and rice on a deer's antlers believing them a running tree, Eulalio drowns nodding at his reflection, Pedro burns a chicken feather-and-all, and Mateo and Francisco kill the old mistress while swatting a fly from her nose — she dies smiling. They roll her body from a flat coffin, bury a live fagot-gathering old woman instead when the priest demands a corpse, and flee in terror at the sight of the 'ghost' they dropped by the roadside.
summary.zh: 七個快活的瘋子捕魚歸來清點人數，胡安漏數自己，以為少了一人，眾人紛紛潛水尋『溺亡』的夥伴，直至老者代為點數並收留他們。此後諸事皆錯：菲elipe把帽與飯掛上鹿角當『會跑的樹』、尤拉利歐向倒影點頭直至溺斃、佩德羅連毛帶炭煮雞、馬特奧與弗朗西斯科打蠅竟打死老婦——她含笑而逝。他們滾落棺中屍體，錯把拾柴老婦活埋，最後見到路旁遺屍驚呼鬼魂，散逃呂宋全島。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan noodle-tale recorded by Fansler from a Mangaldan narrator; archival record. Bicol variant 'Juan and his Six Friends'; Fansler compares the Jataka fly-killing stories and Grimm's 'Seven Swabians.'

passages.text: In the northern part of Luzon lived seven crazy fellows — Juan, Felipe, Mateo, Pedro, Francisco, Eulalio, and Jacinto — happy all the day long. One morning Felipe asked his friends to go fishing, and about two o'clock Mateo said they were hungry and should go home. 'Before we go, let us count ourselves, to see that we are all here!' said Juan — but because he forgot to count himself, he found only six and said one of them had been drowned. All dived into the river for their lost companion; Francisco counted on their emergence and left himself out too, so in they dived again. An old man passing by asked what they were diving for, then counted them properly, and took them into his house as servants.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 9 'The Seven Crazy Fellows'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the hunting trip Felipe, who had never seen a deer, thought the antlers of a standing deer were the branches of a small tree without leaves, and hung his hat and bag of rice on them — but the tree immediately ran away. At home the others fared no better: Eulalio nodded at his own reflection in the well until, tired, he jumped into the water and was drowned; Jacinto destroyed the garden fence instead of gathering sticks; Pedro cooked a chicken without removing the feathers and let it burn black as coal; and Mateo and Francisco, keeping flies off the old mistress's face, struck at one on her nose with big sticks and killed her — she died with seemingly a smile on her face, and the two fools agreed she was very much pleased by their work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 9 'The Seven Crazy Fellows'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They made a flat coffin with nothing to prevent the corpse from falling off, and on the way to the church ran so hard that the body rolled off; running, they agreed, made their burden lighter. When the priest found the corpse missing and sent them back, they met an old woman picking up sticks by the roadside and, binding her, carried her to the church — where the priest, who was also crazy, performed the burial-ceremony over her, answering her cries that she was alive with the remark that since he had her burial-fee he did not care whether she was alive or not. Returning home, they saw the corpse that had fallen from the coffin, and Francisco cried that it was the ghost of the old woman; terribly frightened, they ran away in different directions and became scattered all over Luzon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 9 'The Seven Crazy Fellows'; not verbatim.
